title: The Air Conditioner Problem
passage:
During an unusually hot June, students at Hoshi Junior High complained that several classrooms felt uncomfortable even though the air conditioners were running. The school office responded by lowering the temperature setting. Electricity use rose sharply, yet complaints continued. A science teacher suggested that the school investigate before lowering the setting further. Students in an environmental club borrowed simple temperature and humidity sensors and placed them in different parts of the building. They expected to find broken machines. Instead, the measurements revealed large differences within the same classroom. Desks near sunny windows were several degrees warmer in the afternoon, while areas directly under air outlets felt cold. In one room, the sensor near the teacher's desk showed a comfortable temperature even when students by the windows felt hot. The club also measured carbon dioxide levels as a rough sign of ventilation and found that rooms became stuffy when doors and windows remained closed for long periods. Opening windows improved ventilation but allowed hot outdoor air inside, making cooling harder. The problem was not a single setting. The school tested several changes. Reflective shades were installed on the hottest windows. Fans were used to mix air so cooled air did not remain concentrated in one area. Short ventilation periods were scheduled between lessons instead of leaving windows partly open all the time. Teachers were asked to keep doors closed while cooling unless ventilation was taking place. The school then returned the air conditioner settings closer to their original level. Comfort improved in many rooms, and electricity use fell compared with the first hot week. However, the club avoided claiming that the new system was universally best. Rooms on different floors received different amounts of sun, weather changed daily, and personal comfort varied. One student felt cold at a temperature another considered perfect. The school therefore added a simple reporting form so repeated problems in particular rooms could be identified rather than treating every complaint with the same adjustment. Mina, a club member, was especially interested in what had gone wrong at the beginning. Lowering the temperature setting seemed like a direct response to a heat complaint, but it assumed the air conditioner itself was the main cause. Because no one had measured conditions across the room, the first solution used more energy without addressing uneven sunlight, air movement, or ventilation. Mina began to see a general pattern. When a problem is described by one visible symptom, people often change the most obvious control. Sometimes that works. Other times, the symptom is produced by several interacting factors. Measurement helps separate those possibilities. Yet measurement also has limits: a sensor can report temperature, but it cannot fully measure whether a student feels comfortable, tired, or distracted. The school's final approach combined physical data with human reports. Mina concluded that efficient problem-solving does not mean trusting numbers instead of people or people instead of numbers. It means using each source to answer the kinds of questions it can answer well.

The club repeated measurements on several days and found another lesson: one successful afternoon was not enough evidence for a permanent rule. On cloudy days, the reflective shades made little difference; on bright days, they mattered much more. Fans were useful only when positioned to mix air rather than simply blow papers across desks. The students therefore recorded conditions together with the measurements instead of comparing averages without context. Their questions became more specific. Rather than asking, Do fans work, they asked, Under which conditions, in which rooms, and for which problem do fans help? The answers were less simple but more useful. Staff also kept brief notes about repeated complaints after each adjustment. This habit prevented them from treating every warm room as the same technical problem and made later adjustments faster. It also gave teachers a clearer record of which changes had already been tested.
translation:
非常に暑い六月、星中学校では冷房が動いているのに教室が不快だという苦情が続きました。学校は設定温度を下げましたが、電力使用量だけが急増し、不満はなくなりませんでした。科学の先生の提案で環境部が温度・湿度センサーを教室各所に置くと、故障ではなく同じ教室内で大きな差があることが分かりました。午後の日当たりの強い窓際は数度高く、吹き出し口の真下は寒く感じられました。先生の机付近が適温でも窓側の生徒は暑い場合もありました。また換気の目安として二酸化炭素濃度を測ると、窓や扉を長く閉めると空気がこもる一方、窓を開け続ければ暑い外気が入り冷房効率が落ちます。つまり単一の設定温度の問題ではありませんでした。学校は、日当たりの強い窓に反射シェードを付け、扇風機で空気を混ぜ、授業間に短時間換気を行い、冷房中は換気時以外ドアを閉める方法を試しました。その後設定温度を元に近づけても快適さは改善し、最初の猛暑週より電力消費も減りました。ただし階や日当たり、天候、個人差があるため一つの方法が全教室に最適とは言いませんでした。同じ温度でも寒い人と快適な人がいるからです。そこで教室ごとの繰り返し問題を把握できる報告フォームも作りました。部員の美奈は、最初の失敗に注目しました。暑いという症状に対し設定温度を下げるのは直接的に見えますが、原因が冷房能力だと決めつけていました。教室内を測定しなかったため、日射、空気の偏り、換気を改善せずエネルギーだけ増やしたのです。目立つ症状に対して最も分かりやすい操作を変えるだけで解決することもありますが、複数要因が絡む場合もあります。測定はその違いを見分ける助けになります。ただしセンサーは温度を測れても、生徒の快適さや疲労を完全には測れません。学校は物理データと人の感覚の両方を使いました。効率的な問題解決とは、数字か人のどちらか一方を信じることではなく、それぞれが得意な問いに使うことだと美奈は結論づけました。

部は複数の日に測定を繰り返し、一日の成功例だけでは恒久的なルールを決められないことも学びました。曇天では反射シェードの効果は小さく、晴天では大きくなりました。扇風機も、紙を飛ばすだけの向きではなく空気を混ぜる位置に置いたときに役立ちました。そこで平均値だけを比較するのではなく、その日の条件も一緒に記録しました。問いも『扇風機は効くか』から『どの条件、どの教室、どの問題に効くか』へ具体化しました。答えは単純ではなくなりましたが、実用性は高まりました。調整後の苦情も短く記録し、すべての暑い教室を同じ故障として扱わないようにしました。教師にとっても、すでに何を試したか確認しやすくなりました。
